transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-05-14 10:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Sarah (Acme ML), Tom (Acme infra), Priya (Acme PM)

[00:00] Maya: Okay, good morning everyone, thanks for joining the weekly POC sync. Quick round of intros, we have Daniel from infra and SE side, and on Acme side Sarah, Tom and Priya.
[00:12] Sarah: Hey all, yep, happy to be here.
[00:15] Daniel: morning.
[00:20] Maya: Cool. Agenda — quick run through last week's action items, then we dug into cost metrics and caching results, and then batching tradeoffs, and finish with next steps.
[00:35] Priya: Sounds good.
[00:40] Sarah: One ask — can we keep the spreadsheet up-to-date in the drive?
[00:44] Maya: Yep I'll push the updated cost model after this call.

[02:05] Daniel: Alright, start with the numbers we ran overnight: baseline, no caching, 16k context LLM (open variant), we saw roughly 150k tokens per dollar in the hosted config. With prefix/KV caching enabled we got to about 190k tokens/$ — that's the easy wins. When we enabled both batching and cache tuned for your traffic profile, throughput improved to ~450k tokens per dollar on the dedicated instance.
[02:40] Tom: Wait, 450k tokens per dollar, that's a three x over baseline?
[02:44] Daniel: Yeah, roughly 3x. Caveat is that's under sustained throughput with batching size ~12 and quantized model on the dedicated GPU.
[02:55] Sarah: How does that translate to latency? Our p95 can't go above 800ms.
[03:00] Daniel: Right — so tradeoff: at batch size 12 p50 is nice, like ~220ms, p95 climbs to ~760ms; at batch size 1 p50 is 110ms but tokens/$ drops significantly, down to about 120k tokens/$.
[03:18] Priya: So if we want p95 < 800ms we could operate at batch 8 or 12?
[03:22] Daniel: Correct. Batch 8 gave p50 ~180ms and p95 ~560ms in our run. Batch 12 pushed p95 closer to 760ms. There's also auto-burst settings — small windows where we keep latency low for tail-critical requests and batch for background heavy flows.

[05:10] Maya: On caching — we saw dedupe/prefix caching reduced repeated tokens by about 27% on average for your sample prompts (customer support style prompts with lots of repeated system text). That reduced overall token count and cost accordingly. Note that caching savings vary by prompt distribution; Tom can share the 48h sample and we will re-run.
[05:35] Tom: I'll export that after the meeting. The sample has a lot of short chats and some long sessions.

[06:02] Sarah: Something I noticed — the transcription had a small error last week, it spelled 'KV cache' as K V cash in the notes — just flagging.
[06:10] Maya: Yep our auto notes are imperfect, thanks for flag.

[07:00] Daniel: Another lever is quantization — we ran 8-bit Q8 on the dedicated instance and saw ~20% cost reduction vs FP16, but there was a small drop in answer quality for some prompt categories (multi-step reasoning). We recommend validating on your eval set if you go quant.
[07:20] Priya: For the customer-facing flows, we need to keep quality. Maybe keep FP16 for the high-value paths and quantized for bulk summarization.
[07:28] Daniel: That's the hybrid pattern we recommend.

[09:00] Sarah: Can you explain the tokens/sec per dollar metric again? I want to be precise for finance.
[09:08] Maya: Sure: we calculate total tokens served divided by total cost over a burst window (tokens / $). Practically you can interpret it as how many input+output tokens you get per dollar spent on inference. We've included GPU runtime, transient infra, and model variant cost in the denominator for the dedicated runs; hosted includes API layer fees.
[09:32] Sarah: Example numbers please so we can present to finance.
[09:36] Daniel: Baseline hosted — ~150k tokens/$. Hosted with caching — ~190k tokens/$. Dedicated with batching+cache+quantization (our best-case) — ~450k tokens/$. If you avoid quant and keep FP16 but batch+cache, you're around ~350k tokens/$.
[09:55] Priya: Nice. Is that per GPU-hour or per actual dollar billed?
[09:59] Daniel: Per actual dollar billed as you'd see in the invoice or commit — we normalize to dollars. So it's easier to compare across dedicated or hosted.

[11:10] Tom: Are we including SLOs in the cost calculation? Like cost to keep tail low?
[11:15] Maya: Not directly; cost to maintain lower tail typically increases because you batch less or provision extra capacity. We can model an SLO-adjusted tokens/$ for you once we have the traffic profile — basically a cost delta to hit your p95 target.

[13:00] Sarah: Anything else on reliability? We raised a concern about graceful fallbacks if a dedicated pool is saturated.
[13:08] Daniel: Right, Redwood routing can fallback to a compatible hosted variant or a smaller model; we can configure policies so critical endpoints failover to hosted with slightly higher cost but bounded latency. There's also canary rollouts and automatic scaling to reduce these events.
[13:25] Tom: Good. What about encryption and logs? We need end-to-end encryption and audit logs for compliance.
[13:32] Maya: Private deployment includes KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; Dedicated also supports customer-managed keys via our Private offering. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO docs in the shared folder.

[15:50] Daniel: Back to batching — one important operational thing is burstiness. If traffic is spiky, large fixed batch sizes hurt latency for small bursts. We recommend dynamic batching: a small timer window that flushes early if latency thresholds are approaching. That yields most of the throughput benefits without increasing p95 too much.
[16:12] Priya: Does Redwood support dynamic batching out of the box?
[16:15] Daniel: Yes, configurable. We shipped an autoscale/batching policy that you can tune per-route; Daniel (SE) can provide the config snippet.

[18:40] Sarah: Let's talk about an experiment: run a split config for a week — 70% traffic routed to dedicated with batch=8 and cache enabled; 30% to hosted for low-latency tail. Then evaluate cost & quality. Feasible?
[18:55] Maya: Totally feasible. We'll help set up routing policy and measure tokens/$ across both buckets. Daniel will run the bench and send results.

[21:00] Tom: For the bench, include step-load tests to catch autoscale delays. We saw a slow scale start last month.
[21:08] Daniel: We'll include that. Also we'll instrument request-level tracing so we can see per-request batching and cache hits.

[23:30] Priya: Quick question on model versions: can we pin the model while we iterate? We don't want surprise changes.
[23:36] Maya: Yep you can pin model versions and also pin quantization profiles; rollouts are explicit and we've got canary rules.

[25:00] Daniel: One more note — when we compute tokens/$ we include model warm-start overhead in the first N seconds; for sustained runs it amortizes away, but for short workloads you might see worse tokens/$. We'll include both sustained and transient metrics in the benchmark results.

[27:40] Sarah: Are there any licensing or vendor lock concerns with the quantized models?
[27:45] Daniel: Depends on model license. For the open variants we've used in the POC it's fine; we'll flag any model-specific restrictions in the report.

[30:00] Maya: Ok time for recaps. Action items: Maya to send cost spreadsheet; Daniel to run extended benchmark including caching, batch sizes [1,4,8,12], quantized and non-quantized; Tom to provide traffic sample and SLOs. We'll target to have results by 2025-05-21 and a follow-up deep dive week of 2025-05-26 if needed.
[30:30] Priya: Looks good.

[31:10] Sarah: One thing — can you also include a column that translates tokens/$ into monthly spend projections for our current traffic volume? Finance will love that.
[31:20] Maya: Yes we'll add that to the spreadsheet.

[33:00] Tom: I noticed sometimes the automated transcripts merge speaker labels; e.g., last week it had several "Speaker 1" entries. Not a big deal but just FYI.
[33:07] Maya: Yeah auto attribution can be messy, we'll add manual attendee mapping in the notes.

[35:00] Daniel: Technical note for you Tom — when exporting your traffic sample, include the tokenization breakdown or raw text, we will tokenize it with the exact tokenizer used in the model for accurate cost projection.
[35:12] Tom: Will do.

[37:00] Priya: Any blockers on our side? Sarah: none.
[37:05] Sarah: No blockers.

[38:00] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and the benchmarking plan. If you want a mid-week status I can send a note.
[38:10] Priya: Please do.

[40:00] Maya: Alright thanks everyone, we'll wrap.
[40:05] Sarah: Thanks.
[40:06] Tom: Thanks.
[40:07] Daniel: Thanks all.

End of transcript. Shared artifacts: cost_model.xlsx (link in shared drive), benchmark-config.yaml (snippet), SOC2_summary.pdf (link).
